blogs.title: Standing in the Shadows: Why a FLORA‑Like Case Fails When the Injury Is Information
blogs.description: This post dissects the court’s rigorous application of Article III standing to AFL’s informational claims. We compare AFL’s approach to classic ‘information‑based’ standing (e.g., American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals), highlight the courts’ insistence that a concrete, particularized injury must be traceable to the defendant, and explain why speculative causal chains involving OSC, the Merit Systems Protection Board, and DOJ fail to meet the redressability requirement. The piece also explores the broader trend of courts tightening the bar on informational standing in the digital age.

blogs.title: OSC’s Enforcement Limits: FOIA versus Personnel‑Practice Investigations
blogs.description: This article examines the tension between OSC’s statutory mandates under §1216 (FOIA violations) and §1214/§1215 (prohibited personnel practices). We analyze the court’s conclusion that OSC’s “discretion” under §1216(c) renders AFL’s claim to procedural injury untenable, and discuss how this decision clarifies OSC’s actual investigative scope. The post evaluates the implications for agencies and whistleblowers who might rely on OSC’s enforcement when FOIA and personnel grievances collide.

blogs.title: Relaxed Procedural Injury Standards in D.C. Circuit: A Double‑Edged Sword
blogs.description: Here we unpack the D.C. Circuit’s long‑standing practice of relaxing the standing requirements for procedural injuries—drawing on Ctr. for Law & Educ. v. Dep’t of Educ. and Fla. Audubon Soc’y v. Bentsen. We assess how that doctrine was applied (or not) in AFL’s case, the limits of ‘injury resulting from a procedural right,’ and the court’s decision that AFL failed to show even the relaxed standard. The analysis extends to how this standard may evolve post‑2024 and what it means for litigants seeking procedural redress.

blogs.title: FOIA Policy, Email Searches, and the Edge of Accountability
blogs.description: This post focuses on the policy dispute at the heart of AFL’s FOIA claim: DOJ’s refusal to search employee e‑mail without consent. We explore the statutory framework for FOIA compliance, the potential role of OSC under §1216(a)(3), and why the court found OSC’s refusal to investigate was beneath its mandate. The discussion highlights the broader impact on agency transparency, internal communications, and the balance between privacy and public access.
